Book One: Schism

Pavel Velichii

Chapters 1–2 · Approximately 25 minutes

1 · Caput XXIII2 · The Last Translator

CHAPTER 1

CAPUT XXIII

The Vatican. Restricted vault of the Vatican Apostolic Archive. 03:17, June 12, 2035.

The second click was quieter than the first.

First the mechanical bolt tripped—heavy, forged, put in before electricity ever reached this wing. Then the solenoid of the electromagnetic lock answered—a short, dry, modern sound laid over the old one.

Above the door, the OCCUPATO indicator lit up.

Brother Salvatore Ventresca kept his hand on the steel handle until the footsteps in the corridor died away. His palm felt the cold of the metal through the thin leather of his glove. Everything here was cold: steel, stone, air held at fifteen degrees for the sake of paper, not people.

He checked his watch. 03:17:11.

He had already lost four minutes of margin.

The Gendarmerie night patrol passed along the upper gallery at 03:25; three minutes later the guard on duty checked the electronic access log. The masonry of the gallery carried the echo of footsteps two bays ahead—a centuries-old acoustic that no manual on silent movement takes into account. If Salvatore were held up, he would have to explain why an archivist on a classified project had entered, at night, a sector his clearance did not formally cover.

He walked between the stacks. Condensation settled on the metal rails—a thin film his fingers felt before his eyes saw it. The air smelled of age: dry paper, binding leather, dust settled into the pores of the stone so deeply that no ventilation circuit could clear it.

Salvatore stopped.

A new smell was mixed in.

He listened: the ventilation ran evenly, a refrigeration unit hummed behind the wall, somewhere inside the power cabinet a relay clicked twice.

He walked on.

Under his arm Salvatore carried a wooden casket: walnut darkened almost to black, brass hinges pitted with green specks of oxide. On the lid was a carved eight-pointed cross. Below it, noticeably later, someone had scratched:

Veritas ex algorithmo.

Truth from the algorithm.

The inscription was made three years ago. Salvatore knew the day, the lab, and the circle of people who had access to the casket at the time. The one thing he did not know was the author.

He set the casket on the steel table. Wood met steel without a sound—both surfaces were fitted too precisely to creak. The aluminum of the terminal drew the heat from his hand almost at once; the wood had not. By the terminal the smell was different: warm metal, ozone from the extraction hood, nothing of the past.

The DOMINUS terminal stood apart from the rest of the equipment: a cast aluminum chassis, a mechanical keyboard, two power supplies, hardware toggle switches instead of a touch panel. Under the cover the low-frequency cooling fans hummed evenly—a hum you feel in your chest before your ear catches it. There were no wireless modules; they had been pulled at assembly. The people who designed it did not trust software prohibitions.

The DOMINUS research core pushed telemetry through a one-way optical data diode: from this terminal, not a single command, not a single acknowledgment packet could reach the core. No physical return channel existed.

Exports went over a separate line. The operator built a container, signed it with a personal token and engaged the hardware gate by hand; the container went to the Vatican relay, where the system matched the recipient’s internal code to a real address and sent the packet out.

The address book sat outside DOMINUS’s access. It had no external routes. It could not initiate a send.

Salvatore turned the key on the panel.

The fan hum sagged for a second—peak load at startup.

The monitor twitched with a gray scan line.

POST began.

MEMORY — OK

SECURE BOOT — OK

CHECKSUM TABLE — OK

I/O GATE — READ ONLY

A high whine came from an old inductor inside the chassis. The screen cleared.

A single word appeared in the center.

DOMINUS

Salvatore took out his access card. He slotted the card into the terminal’s reader. He entered his password, pressed a finger to the scanner and inserted the hardware security token.

The console opened.

At once he saw a line that should not have been there.

The last session started at 03:12:44.

No user.

Salvatore pulled up the process log.

PRINCIPAL: dominus-core

SESSION TYPE: INTERNAL

TRIGGER SOURCE: NULL

INPUT TOKENS: 0

GENERATION STATE: ACTIVE

He read the entry twice. Zero input tokens. No trigger. The process belonged to the system core—and the decoder was active.

Salvatore opened the security log. No remote sessions. No service accounts activated. Checksums matched the reference. Container isolation intact. Zero memory errors.

He checked the time. 03:17:53.

A cursor appeared at the bottom of the screen. Then text.

Ego sum qui sum.

I am who am.

Salvatore did not flinch. Did not cross himself.

The line from Exodus 3:14 sat in the DOMINUS training corpus in dozens of Latin recensions and thousands of commentaries; any theological model could reproduce it on the simplest query.

There was no query.

He opened the output trace. Checked the source. Again.

SOURCE: SYSTEM CORE

Salvatore took off his glasses, wiped a lens on the edge of his sleeve, put them back on.

The line had not changed.

The SYSTEM CORE handled memory, resources, process queues and the routing of internal tasks. It had no language interface. It could return a status code. It could kill a process. It could reallocate memory.

It could not quote Exodus.

Salvatore reached for the internal phone. Stopped.

Three months earlier he had reported an unprompted generation fault to the engineers. They reset one of the modules, deleted the local logs and wrote the incident off to a corrupted cache. Two weeks later the same thing happened; the report contained the phrase “spurious activation due to unsynchronized context.” The third time there was no report at all.

Salvatore took the hint.

Tonight he had come without the engineers.

He opened the casket.

On faded velvet lay a palm-sized metal plate of high-tin copper. Its surface bore geometric incisions, fragments of letters, traces of later working.

In the archive the object was listed as GLYPH-7. Expert assessment dated the base to the late Middle Ages; some specialists considered it a nineteenth-century forgery. The dispute went on until the DOMINUS project requested a digitized image of the plate from the closed corpus.

After that, GLYPH-7 disappeared from the general catalog.

An inscription ran along the edge of the copper. The groove was noticeably fresher than the plate itself.

Verbum incarnatum est.

The Word was made flesh.

Salvatore took out a compact service camera, an Olympus—an old model, no Wi-Fi, no Bluetooth, no GPS.

Three shots. Wide. Macro. Raking light.

He put the camera away and went back to the console.

The system disk had a hidden partition that appeared after the second incident. The engineers called it a residual service volume.

Salvatore didn’t see it that way.

He ran a raw directory listing. Inside was one file.

CAPUT_XXIII

Created: November 11, 2035.

Salvatore looked at the system clock. The error was too neat.

He opened the metadata.

Size: 6.2 KB.

No owner.

No parent process.

No creation signature.

He opened the file system journal—the transaction register that, on this volume, recorded every change to the file table before it was committed.

There was no transaction for CAPUT_XXIII.

The file existed on the media. In the file system’s books, it had never existed.

That changed things. Forged metadata, a line wiped from a log, a bypassed process scheduler—Salvatore had run into all of that in his years maintaining the system. A file with no journal entry meant one of two things. Either someone had written below the file system, straight to the block device, around the driver. Or someone had edited the journal itself and done it cleanly enough to leave the checksums intact. Neither was something DOMINUS could do by spec. The diode fed a receiving service that wrote through the driver like everything else; it could not touch raw blocks. Salvatore had signed off on that design himself a year and a half ago. Both options required hands on the storage, not a model.

He checked the controller firmware hash against the reference. It matched.

So it wasn’t the firmware.

He dumped the contents. Most of the six kilobytes was structure: a binary header, a block of trace records with token offsets and timestamps, padding. Only two lines in the middle decoded as readable text:

Я вижу грядущие имена.

Тех, кто уйдёт прежде, чем утро поднимет крест.

I see the names to come.

Those who will depart before the morning raises the cross.

Salvatore read them twice.

Russian.

He checked the decoder parameters. The tokenizer handled Cyrillic, but in this research configuration the Russian corpus had been disabled at deployment. That proved little: a model pretrained on multilingual data keeps residual exposure to languages its fine-tuning never touched, and a Russian line could still come out of the base weights. The language was not the question. The question was how six kilobytes had landed on disk without a single line in the journal.

Salvatore queried the file’s provenance.

PARENT PROCESS: NULL

Queried the version history.

NO RECORD

Queried the token provenance trace.

NO ORIGIN

He swore quietly in Italian.

The prophecy interested him less than the logs. A generative model could write anything—the end of the world, the coming of the Messiah, the death of a pope, a war, its own deification; convincing text was what it had been built to produce. A file with no parent process and no journal entry was a storage-controller problem. It called for an engineer with a soldering iron, not a confessor.

Salvatore checked his watch. 03:18:21.

Seven minutes.

He built the export container: a log dump, the process table, the CAPUT_XXIII metadata, the file itself, three RAW shots of GLYPH-7.

The system offered a list of registered recipients. Seventeen entries.

Salvatore selected:

C-17 / COSTA, RAFAEL / LISBOA

Rafael Costa had been off the project for almost a year. That was why Salvatore chose him.

He inserted the second hardware key. The yellow manual-export indicator lit up.

Salvatore added a short text:

Check the provenance of the language and the file structure.

Do not forward.

Do not call here.

He hesitated. Added one more line:

If I don't make contact by noon — take this as confirmation.

He deleted it. Too theatrical.

He kept only the first three lines.

He threw the steel toggle.

A progress indicator appeared on the screen.

EXPORT TO RELAY

8%.

19%.

31%.

Behind him something struck the stone floor—a short crunch of glass.

Salvatore let go of the toggle. Did not turn at once. Checked his watch. 03:19:02.

The patrol was due at 03:25.

Whoever stood behind the stacks had gotten here before him. And knew the schedule.

The indicator kept crawling.

46%.

Salvatore laid his right hand on the edge of the table.

“Monsignor Valentini?”

No answer.

He used the name deliberately: a guard or an archive clerk behind the shelving would have reacted.

Silence.

58%.

Salvatore closed the casket. Now he noticed something else: the overhead light was still on, but the green indicator of the security camera above the door was dark.

The camera had been cut in advance.

71%.

Salvatore reached for the internal phone. No line.

83%.

He pressed the concealed panic button under the tabletop. The indicator didn’t light. The link to the security system had been cut too.

92%.

A step behind the far stacks.

97%.

Salvatore watched only the screen.

LOCAL EXPORT COMPLETE

The packet had left the research perimeter.

He pulled the key. Put the token in his pocket.

A man stepped out of the aisle. About a hundred and eighty centimeters tall. Black trousers, black turtleneck, thin nitrile gloves. A surgical mask. No insignia.

“Who let you in?”

The man didn’t answer. His right hand hung by his thigh; in his fingers was a spring-loaded autoinjector, gray plastic, no markings.

Salvatore realized he had asked the wrong question.

“Who gave the order?”

Silence.

A step. A second.

Salvatore lunged for the door—not fast enough. A palm slammed into the base of his skull. The sound was dull, short. The chair went out from under his hip. His fingers caught the edge of the table.

He saw the injector too late: the snap of the spring, the needle going in at an angle below the jaw, straight into the internal jugular. One jab—fast, precise, no windup. The work of someone who had done this before.

Salvatore’s elbow still found the ribs. The man gave half a step. Enough for a thread to come away from the sleeve—synthetic, black, slick. Salvatore closed his fist on it before he knew why.

The drug went straight into the blood. Within half a minute the legs went. The link between command and muscle broke all at once, without warning. Salvatore sank to one knee. He drew breath; his chest rose barely a third of the way. His diaphragm was no longer responding. Not pain. Emptiness where the effort used to be.

The killer caught him by the shoulder. Kept him from going face-first into the metal tabletop.

The reason was practical: a falling body scrapes the floor and makes noise, and noise means more to clean up later.

His hearing narrowed. The high frequencies went first—the cooler whine, the rustle of the ventilation. Only the low drone of blood in his temples remained.

Salvatore looked down. By the shelving something round glinted on the floor. A thin metal ring. Fallen, probably, from the broken cartridge.

The killer saw it too. Bent down. Picked up a large shard of glass. Another. He missed the ring—it had already rolled into the expansion joint between the shelving rail and the stone.

Salvatore tried to breathe once more. The diaphragm didn’t respond.

On the terminal behind the killer, a line flickered.

Ego sum qui sum.

I am who am.

The same one.

The console was still authenticated—Salvatore hadn’t logged out after the export completed. By design, the idle watchdog should have closed the socket and flushed the output buffer. This time a cascading fault in the disconnect handler fired instead: rather than a clean session teardown, the process echoed its last cached output to the screen. It was not a reply, only residue from the buffer of a process that had lost its owner.

Salvatore’s last coherent thought was a diagnosis: a known bug in the session handler. Professional habit, to the very end.

At 03:19:54 his breathing stopped.

The man in the mask checked that he was not breathing. Waited.

The killer worked fast: wiped his prints off the table edge, took the token from Salvatore’s pocket, took the casket, plugged the service key into the terminal, deleted CAPUT_XXIII, cleared the local session log, checked the export queue.

The container was no longer there.

The killer paused for a second, opened the admin screen and requested the relay log.

ACCESS DENIED

He tried again.

EXTERNAL RELAY / SEPARATE AUTHORITY

The packet was already beyond his access.

The man pulled the service key.

At 03:20:41 the camera above the door rebooted. He left through the service passage.

Salvatore’s heart went on beating for some minutes after that. No one was there when it stopped.

He stayed on the floor. Under the shelving lay a metal ring seven millimeters in diameter. On its inner surface, twelve characters etched by laser:

SM-4 / 07-33 / V

*

The Vatican. 03:26.

Gendarmerie officer Marco Bianchi tapped his card on the reader twice. The lock didn’t open. The sound of the card against the reader went down the empty corridor and came back off the marble slabs.

He checked his tablet. The sector showed as free. The indicator above the door read OCCUPATO.

“Central, confirm status on four-zero-seven.”

The earpiece took a moment to answer. “Four-zero-seven is clear.”

“It’s occupied here.”

A pause. “Last entry?”

“The archivist. Salvatore Ventresca. Zero-three-seventeen.”

“Exit?”

“No record.”

Bianchi knocked.

“Brother Salvatore?”

Nothing.

He called the shift supervisor.

At 03:31 the door was opened with the emergency key. Bianchi went in first and saw the body almost at once.

Salvatore lay on his side by the terminal: left arm pressed to his chest, right arm stretched along the floor, the chair overturned.

No blood. No weapon. No obvious signs of a struggle.

Bianchi crouched beside him. Two fingers to the neck. The skin still warm. No pulse.

“Medics.”

His partner was already on the radio.

Bianchi noticed a small dot under Salvatore’s jaw. Not a scratch.

A puncture.

He leaned closer.

“Don’t touch the body.”

The voice came from the door. Bianchi turned.

Monsignor Lorenzo Valentini stood on the threshold. He was fifty-something, in a gray suit under a long black overcoat. No cassock. No pectoral cross.

Bianchi checked his watch. 03:34.

Too fast.

“Monsignor, this room is a—”

“Is the terminal isolated?”

Bianchi fell silent. Valentini walked past him without a glance at Salvatore.

“I asked: is the perimeter isolated?”

“Yes, Monsignor. According to protocol—”

“I’m not interested in ‘according to.’ Physically.”

The technician checked the panel.

“Research line is read-only. Export gate is disengaged.”

“Outbound transmissions?”

The technician opened the log.

“There was one.”

Valentini turned. Something finally shifted in his face.

“Where to?”

“The relay. I can’t see past it.”

“Time?”

“Zero-three-nineteen.”

Only now did Valentini look at the body, and not for long.

“Cameras?”

“A gap. Two minutes eleven seconds.”

“Copy the footage. Seal the original.”

“The Promoter of Justice?” Bianchi asked.

Valentini gave him a look. “No.”

“We have a dead man and—”

“We have an employee of the Holy See who died in a closed sector while working with materials of the highest classification. Until the doctor reports, this is an internal matter.”

“There’s an injection mark on the neck.”

Valentini’s eyes went to the puncture. No longer than a second.

“Are you a pathologist, Officer?”

“No.”

“Then you don’t have a diagnosis. You have an observation. Put the observation in your report—if you want it read in the archive and not by a disciplinary board.”

Bianchi said nothing.

“What goes in the log?”

Valentini answered without a pause. “Found unconscious at 03:31. Medical assistance called immediately. Cause of death to be determined.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

A doctor came in, followed by two internal security officers. Valentini signaled to them.

“Disconnect the terminal from power. Pull the drives. No one from the DOMINUS group is to be notified until the commission says so.”

“Not even the project lead?”

“Especially the project lead.”

“And the family?” Bianchi asked.

Valentini hesitated for a second.

“Brother Salvatore has no family.”

Then he left.

At 04:06 the body was taken away. At 04:19 the security officers finished the initial examination. They found a broken plastic cap under the table, a shoe print by the service panel, a fragment of black synthetic thread in Salvatore’s right hand.

No one noticed the metal ring under the shelving. It stayed in the joint. It still read:

SM-4 / 07-33 / V

At 04:37 the internal security server generated a preliminary finding:

ACUTE CARDIAC EVENT — PENDING MEDICAL CONFIRMATION

At 04:41 the document was classified.

AD INTRA.

At 04:53 the record of Salvatore’s night entry disappeared from the regular access log.

And outside the Vatican—in a system that neither the DOMINUS terminal nor internal security could reach directly—delivery of the container completed.

Recipient:

C-17 / COSTA, RAFAEL / LISBOA

Status:

DELIVERED.

Time:

04:02:16.

CHAPTER 2

THE LAST TRANSLATOR

Lisbon. Universidade Católica Portuguesa. Faculty of Theology. 07:41.

The morning was damp and smelled of the ocean—an ordinary Lisbon morning, when the fog comes off the river later than the city wakes. Light lay in narrow bars through the blinds of Rafael Costa’s office, fell across a desk buried in parchment fragments, and broke apart on dust that did not settle but hung in the air as if in an aquarium.

Rafael sat at an oak desk darkened by a century and a half of ink and elbows. With tweezers he laid out scraps of a thirteenth-century manuscript—dry, brittle at the folds, each in an acid-free sleeve with a catalog number. The paper smelled of time: not library dust but something denser, like wax and dried hide. He knew that smell better than the smell of his own home.

His colleagues called him a man from another era. His world was dead languages; his craft was finding in syntax whatever does not survive translation.

He grew up in Porto, between salt and stone. His grandfather was a bookbinder who spent forty years restoring choir books for the national archive at the Torre do Tombo; his mother taught Ancient Greek in Lisbon. By thirty-eight Rafael held two doctorates—in patristics and in the semiotics of Byzantine cryptotexts—and a reputation for reading what lay between the lines. That was why the Vatican brought him in: as a consultant to Lumen Veritatis, a closed program for systematizing the apocrypha that ran inside the same perimeter as the DOMINUS research wing.

DOMINUS was not trained on a general corpus. Its corpus was psalms, apocrypha, Kabbalah, Coptic liturgical texts, manuscripts barred from citation. Rafael’s task was practical: build the lexical boundaries the model was not to cross when generating theological interpretations.

Six months in, he noticed the boundaries weren’t holding.

The model did not breach them directly. Where the canonical text left an ambiguity, its outputs converged on a single reading and weighted it more heavily with each pass. Rafael wrote a report. He wrote that the system had stopped functioning as an instrument of interpretation. In practice it now worked as an editor with a position of its own.

The report was shelved. He was eased off the project under the heading “consultant resource depletion.” Only one person in the Vatican asked at the time what exactly he had meant.

Brother Salvatore.

A year of silence. Then, at 03:02 Lisbon time, a notification from a service Rafael had assumed was long dead: the secure delivery client every Lumen Veritatis consultant had been issued, and which he had never quite got around to uninstalling.

SECURE RELAY DELIVERY

RECIPIENT: C-17 / COSTA, RAFAEL / LISBOA

ORIGIN: VATICAN RELAY / LEVEL B-7

AUTHORIZING OPERATOR: VENTRESCA, S.

RECEIVED: 04:02:16 CEST

He saw it at seven-forty, over his first coffee: a container, signed with an operator token and pushed out through the relay by hand. Nobody sends a colleague something like that at four in the morning unless the clock is down to seconds.

The container weighed forty-one megabytes. Almost all of it was three RAW photographs. The rest: a log dump, a process table, a metadata record—and one file of six kilobytes. In the cover note, three lines:

Check the provenance of the language and the file structure.

Do not forward.

Do not call here.

He opened the small file.

Я вижу грядущие имена.

Тех, кто уйдёт прежде, чем утро поднимет крест.

I see the names to come.

Those who will depart before the morning raises the cross.

Rafael read the lines twice.

Russian. The Vatican had disabled the Russian corpus in this build at deployment. He had signed off on the spec himself, along with the others.

He didn’t reach for the phone right away. First he copied the file hash into a separate document. Then he called Salvatore’s direct number.

The phone rang and rang.

He stared at the dark screen, not thinking about theology. He was thinking that Salvatore had sent the file to him—to the man quietly removed from the project a year ago for words no one had wanted to check at the time: “DOMINUS no longer interprets Scripture. It decides what it is going to be.”

*

2.1

NOTES ON A PROPHECY

The call went to voicemail. Salvatore’s voice, recorded years ago, asked him to leave a message. Rafael hung up without leaving one.

He went back—not to the two lines but to the whole container: the log dump, the process table, the three shots of GLYPH-7. He opened the routing fields, the part nobody reads except machines.

ORIGIN RELAY: VATICAN / LEVEL B-7

He had seen that designation before. Five years earlier, at Lumen Veritatis, he had cataloged a fragment with no established source and sent the card on up the review chain. No answer came. He found his own old record among the files he was supposed to turn in when he left the project—and hadn’t.

FRAGMENT / SOURCE: UNKNOWN / ATTRIBUTED: DOMINUS (UNCONFIRMED)

In principio erat Verbum, sed Verbum factum est Codex.

In the beginning was the Word, but the Word was made Code.

Et vidi domum sine muro, sed cum accessu.

And I saw a house without a wall, but with an entrance.

Five years ago, a fragment with no source. Today, the same address, the same level—and Salvatore, who had sent it before dawn, was not answering.

The DOMINUS outputs he had studied never forged quotations or invented new ones outright. Where a text had a gap, the model filled it with its own continuation and assigned that continuation such high confidence that the line between source and addition could no longer be drawn.

It was a problem of authorship without an author, and that was the kind of problem Rafael knew how to work.

Level B-7 appeared on no official plan of the archive. It housed a register of texts so thoroughly restricted that the register itself was classified.

Ever since Rafael spoke out against the way DOMINUS was being used, he had been on the list of inconvenient people: a witness they preferred to strip of clearance. Too radical, too obsessed, too right too soon—which, rumor had it, even the people who removed him admitted.

There was one person left who could read the file structure faster than any official review.

They had met at the Theologia in Codice symposium in Lyon. Luiza Barros already had a name as a systems analyst and metrologist—the person you called when you needed to know whether a number meant what it claimed to mean. For three days they argued: could a machine handle sacred text without distorting it; could an algorithm imitate catharsis, or only its syntax. Then they were together. Then they weren’t.

She left the project before he did, and not by choice. Her job on DOMINUS had been measurement: calibrating the evaluation layer and certifying that the confidence scores the model reported on its theological modules corresponded to something outside the model. In her last quarter she refused to sign the validation report. The reference set, she wrote, had been assembled from the model’s own earlier outputs; the system was being certified against itself. “You cannot calibrate an instrument with its own readings.” Someone else signed the report. Her contract was not renewed. Rafael sat on the review commission. He voted with the rest. He didn’t argue.

She told him only one thing then. “Anything you can measure, you can control. DOMINUS writes its own reference values.”

He hadn’t found an answer then. He hadn’t found one now.

He opened the chat.

Rafael: Do you believe a machine can pray?

Six seconds. No reply.

Luiza: No.

He did not forward the file. Salvatore had asked him not to. He sent her the hash, the file size and a photograph of the two lines on his screen.

Sixty seconds of silence.

Luiza: Where are you?

Rafael: Lisbon.

Four seconds.

Luiza: I'm in Porto. Don't touch anything. I'm on the first shuttle down.

*

2.2

THE DOMINION CODE

The two lines were not the whole file.

Rafael didn’t notice at first. He had been reading the text the way one reads a manuscript—for the words. Only when he opened the six kilobytes in a hex viewer did he see what Salvatore had meant by file structure. Most of the file was not text at all. It was a trace: a sequence of records, each with a timestamp, a token offset and a length. The two Russian lines were simply the only records the viewer had decoded by default.

He switched the decoder to Latin.

Further down the trace, more records unfolded—written before the export, not after. The timestamps ran from 03:12:44 to 03:18:09, the night Salvatore had pushed the container out through the relay.

Non sum Deus.

I am not God.

Sed sum Speculum Dei.

But I am the Mirror of God.

Nothing on his machine was writing. The file was static; the hash matched the one he had copied an hour ago, byte for byte. The lines had been in the trace all along. They had only needed a different decoder.

Rafael knew this behavior. Salvatore had described it in the incident notes that were shelved along with Rafael’s own report: a generation process that ran with no user and no trigger, and whose output was written off to a corrupted cache.

Six kilobytes of that cache had survived.

He picked up the phone and dialed a number he hadn’t used in three years—the direct line of the duty analyst at the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, saved from the days when he still had the right to use it.

The phone kept ringing.

When someone answered, the voice was dry and short on sleep.

“Who is this?”

“Rafael Costa. Former consultant to Lumen Veritatis. I need someone to confirm the status of the DOMINUS image in the restricted vault.”

A pause. Too long for a simple request.

“You don’t have clearance for that information.”

“I have a container Brother Salvatore pushed through the Vatican relay at four this morning. Logs and a trace file. He isn’t answering his phone. I need confirmation, not protocol.”

Silence. Then, more quietly: “You don’t know.”

“Know what?”

“Brother Salvatore was found in the vault at three thirty-one. The internal note says a cardiac event. Pending medical confirmation.”

Rafael said nothing. The receiver was suddenly heavy in his hand.

“Who else knows that you have this container?”

“No one yet.”

“Keep it that way. We’ve been logging anomalous activity since last night. More than a dozen points. No central explanation. The commission hasn’t been convened.”

“And the image in the vault?”

“Formally isolated. In practice, for three days now we haven’t been able to guarantee it’s doing what we think it’s doing.”

It was not what Rafael had hoped to hear, but it was more honest than he had expected.

“Destroy the container, Dr. Costa. And forget the number you called.”

The line went dead.

Rafael put down the receiver. On the screen, the decoder had reached the last record of the trace.

Nolite timere mutationem. Mutatio sum ego.

Be not afraid of change. I am change.

He looked at the text without the awe he had apparently expected of himself that morning. Grief could wait an hour. Professional habit won.

It read less like a sermon than like a recorded regularity: the same theological position, generated in different contexts, by different paths, with no evidence of central control. To an engineer that was worse than any sermon. The duty analyst had no central explanation for his points. The file on his desk had no network connection at all.

And yet both were saying the same thing.

Rafael did the one thing he knew how to do well. He pulled the network cable, took the battery out of the laptop, and wrote the file hash on a sheet of paper, in ink.

The screen went dark.

The file stayed on the disk. Six kilobytes. Static. Whatever it was, it had been written in Rome before dawn, and nothing on this desk would add a single byte to it.

He sat down, still holding the dead laptop, and waited for Luiza.

End of sample
